y-m-72-01.title: Her salary went up, but is her household better off?
y-m-72-01.topic: Nominal income and real purchasing power (reflecting prices)
y-m-72-01.goal: Confirm with numbers that the rate at which a salary rose alone cannot tell whether a household is better off, and that the conclusion can change depending on average prices and the makeup of my spending, and revise your judgment.
y-m-72-01.material: Ms. Hana is an office worker and her salary went up this year. In this task, 'her household got better off' means 'the amount of goods she can buy with the same salary increased'. Do not consider taxes, savings, interest or changes in the quality of goods. Information is revealed step by step, and you may keep or revise the judgment you made at one step after seeing the next information.
y-m-72-01.thinking.0: Revising your judgment and confidence as information increases
y-m-72-01.thinking.1: Finding a claim that lacks something to compare with
y-m-72-01.thinking.2: Telling apart averages and individual cases
y-m-72-01.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. You know the meaning of percentages and rates of increase and can calculate with decimals (about Grade 7 to 8 level). This task is at an introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your judgment about 'did Ms. Hana's household get better off?'
y-m-72-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write on one line each the numbers that are known and what is not yet known.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.hint.1: Let last year's price of goods be 100, write what this year's price of goods and salary are, then compare the salary and the price of goods on the same scale.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Ms. Hana's salary rose 3%, from 300만원 last year to 309만원 this year. (There is no other information yet.)
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only what is known now, how would you judge whether the amount of goods she can buy with the same salary has increased?
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The salary going up alone does not let you conclude her household got better off. You need to know how much the price of goods rose in the same period. It is fine to tentatively think 'it probably increased', but you should leave it as a judgment that can change.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I think it increased because the salary went up
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Looking at the salary number alone, it looks that way. But the amount she can buy also depends on the price of goods. Find what information is missing.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: I cannot decide yet because I do not know the price of goods
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that points out that information needed for the comparison is missing.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I take it as increased for now, but I will change it when information about the price of goods comes out
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that sets a tentative judgment together with the conditions under which it will change.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 3% is a small number, so I think it decreased
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Whether 3% is small depends on what it is compared with. There is nothing to compare with yet.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.info: In the same period, the average price level (consumer prices) in the region where Ms. Hana lives rose 4%.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Compared with last year, roughly how did the amount of goods she can buy with this year's salary change?
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If last year's price of goods is 100, this year's is 104, and the salary rose from 300 to 309. In terms of last year's prices, 309÷1.04≈297.1만원 worth, about 1% less than last year's salary (300만원). (Estimating 3%−4%=−1% gives a similar result.) Based on average prices, her household got a little worse off.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a value that looks only at the rate at which the salary rose. Check whether you took into account that the price of goods also rose.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You must not add 3% and 4%. The salary and the price of goods act in opposite directions.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The salary rose 3% and the price of goods rose 4%, so the price of one item grew faster than the salary.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a value that looks only at the rate at which prices rose. Check whether you took into account that the salary also rose.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Looking at Ms. Hana's spending makeup last year: rent 50% (the contract is fixed, so the same amount this year), food 20% (up 8% this year), and the rest 30% (up 4% this year).
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Looking not at average prices but at Ms. Hana's own spending makeup, how did the amount she can buy with her salary change?
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Ms. Hana's own rate of price increase is 0.5×0%+0.2×8%+0.3×4%=2.8%. Her salary rose 3%, so 309÷1.028≈300.6만원 worth, about the same as last year or a tiny bit more. Even in the same society, 'my own prices' can differ if the spending makeup differs. Choosing average prices was a right judgment for an average household, but in Ms. Hana's case the new information changes the judgment.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a value that looked only at the rent being fixed and thought the salary raise stays whole. Food and the other spending went up.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a value that used the average prices as they were. Check again whether Ms. Hana's spending makeup is the same as the average.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a value that looked only at the 4% price rise. It has not yet taken into account that rent did not go up.
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: About the same, or increased by a tiny bit
y-m-72-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This agrees with the result of comparing the rate of price increase for Ms. Hana (about 2.8%), weighted by her spending shares, with the salary increase rate (3%).
y-m-72-01.s.s1.reflect: The judgment about Ms. Hana changed, or became more concrete, from 'salary only' to 'average prices' to 'her own spending makeup'. Say what new information became known at each step that changed the judgment. Could things still unknown (taxes, savings, changes in the quality of goods) change the conclusion again?
y-m-72-01.s.s2.prompt: A friend says, 'My salary went up 5%, so my household is much better off now.' Write one or two things you would want to ask your friend, and how the conclusion could change depending on the answers.
y-m-72-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find where the friend's statement lacks something to compare with.
y-m-72-01.s.s2.hint.1: Divide into three cases where the same 5% is paired with prices rising 3%, 5% and 8%, and write the conclusion for each.
y-m-72-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do the questions I wrote make clear what should be compared with 'the rate at which the salary rose'?
y-m-72-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I write concrete conditions (for example more or less than 5%) for how the conclusion changes when the answer differs?
y-m-72-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I think about the fact that my own spending makeup may differ from the average?
y-m-72-01.s.s2.model.0: I would like to ask by what percent prices rose, and how much the rent or food you mainly spend on went up. If prices rose by less than 5%, then your buying power did increase, but if they rose by more than 5%, it actually decreased.
y-m-72-01.s.s2.model.1: If a big expense like rent stayed the same, your household might change less even when average prices rise, so I would like to know how the prices of the things you often buy changed. If they rose by more than 5%, the conclusion would change.
y-m-72-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It is good that you used the concrete rate of 5% as the standard for comparison.

y-m-72-02.title: Can we say a bigger package is always cheaper?
y-m-72-02.topic: Comparing unit prices and spending decisions
y-m-72-02.goal: Find the price per unit to show that the generalization 'the bigger, the cheaper' does not hold, and say what else you need to know besides the prices to decide whether it is really a better deal.
y-m-72-02.material:
A store sells the same detergent in three sizes on the same day. 
Small 500mL: 4,000원
Medium 1,500mL: 11,400원
Large 3,000mL: 24,000원
(Read: 500 milliliters, 4,000원; 1,500 milliliters, 11,400원; 3,000 milliliters, 24,000원.) Seoyun said, 'The bigger the package, the cheaper the price for the same amount, so you should always buy the large one.'
y-m-72-02.thinking.0: Checking a generalization by putting several values side by side
y-m-72-02.thinking.1: Telling apart sufficient information and needed information
y-m-72-02.thinking.2: Making several values that fit the conditions
y-m-72-02.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience finding a price per unit as price ÷ amount (decimal calculation, Grade 7 level). This task is at an introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-02.s.s1.prompt: This is Seoyun's memo. Check whether all the calculations are right, and choose the one line whose reasoning is lacking.
y-m-72-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write the results of the three lines, 8, 7.6, 8, side by side in the order of package size.
y-m-72-02.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether the value keeps going down from the small package to the large one, or whether it goes up somewhere in the middle.
y-m-72-02.s.s1.line.3: So the bigger the package, the cheaper the price for the same amount.
y-m-72-02.s.s1.explain: The calculations in lines 1 to 3 are all correct. The problem is line 4. The price for the same amount is 8 for small, 7.6 for medium and 8 for large, so it does not keep getting cheaper as the package gets bigger. Medium is the cheapest, and large is more expensive than medium and equal to small. If you put the three values side by side and look at the change, you can see where 'the bigger' does not hold.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.prompt: Even after seeing the results, Seoyun says, 'Still, I should buy the large one.' To decide which purchase is the best deal, what else do you need to know besides this table? Choose all that apply.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.hint.0: Suppose you bought the large 3,000mL, and write how many days it would last at the amount you use per day at home.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine what happens if that number of days is longer than the period you can use the product.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.o.a: The amount used in a month and the period the product can be used
y-m-72-02.s.s2.r.a: If you buy more than you use, the remainder may be thrown away. Then the money you actually paid becomes large compared with the amount you used.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.o.b: The space to store it and the money you can pay at one time
y-m-72-02.s.s2.r.b: A large package costs a lot of money at once and takes up space. Even if it is cheaper per unit, whether you can handle that affects the choice.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.o.c: The prices at another store selling the same detergent
y-m-72-02.s.s2.r.c: Another store's prices help in deciding where to buy, but they are not information you need to compare the package sizes at this store.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.o.d: The result of calculating the price per mL of small, medium and large once more
y-m-72-02.s.s2.r.d: You already found these values. It is not new information; it is looking at the same information again.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.explain: The price per unit compares only 'the price of the same amount'. Whether it is really a better deal also depends on the amount you can use up, the period you can use it, and storage and the money you can pay at one time. Knowing another store's prices is useful for deciding where to buy.
y-m-72-02.s.s2.acc.0: If you know the prices at another store too, you can also decide where to buy. It is not strictly needed to choose the package size at this store, but it is information worth considering together.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.prompt: Medium is 11,400원 and small is 4,000원. Set a new price p for large, and make three different prices for which large is more expensive per same amount than medium but cheaper than small. (Prices are integers in units of 100원.)
y-m-72-02.s.s3.hint.0: First find, one each, the price at which large becomes exactly as cheap as medium and the price at which it becomes exactly equal to small.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.hint.1: Pick a value in units of 100원 between those two prices and find the price per mL directly to check.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.ok.c1: The price is a positive integer in units of 100원.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make the price a positive integer in units of 100원.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.ok.c2: The price per mL of large is more expensive than medium (7.6원).
y-m-72-02.s.s3.fail.c2: The price per mL of large is not more expensive than medium's 7.6원. First find how much 3,000mL would cost at medium's price per mL.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.ok.c3: The price per mL of large is cheaper than small (8원).
y-m-72-02.s.s3.fail.c3: The price per mL of large is not cheaper than small's 8원. Find how much 3,000mL would cost at small's price per mL.
y-m-72-02.s.s3.explain: Buying 3,000mL at medium's 7.6원/mL is 22,800원, and at small's 8원/mL it is 24,000원. If the large price is greater than 22,800원 and less than 24,000원 (for example 23,000원), it is more expensive than medium and cheaper than small. In this way, package size and price per unit do not always move in the same direction.

y-m-72-03.title: If income rises, does the money you take home go down?
y-m-72-03.topic: Tax rates by bracket and after-tax income (progressive rule)
y-m-72-03.goal: Correctly apply the point that when you cross a bracket boundary the new tax rate applies only to the part over the boundary, not to the whole income, and build examples yourself where after-tax income rises even though the average tax rate goes up.
y-m-72-03.material:
The following is an imaginary income tax rule made for this task (it is not a real tax law). Annual income (in 만원) is divided into brackets, and each bracket's rate applies only to the amount that belongs to that bracket.
- The part up to 4,000만원: 10%
- The part over 4,000만원 and up to 8,000만원: 20%
- The part over 8,000만원: 30%
The tax is the sum of the taxes on these three parts, and after-tax income is income minus tax. Seoyun solved it saying, 'Once you go over 4,000만원 the rate becomes 20%, so you actually lose.'
y-m-72-03.thinking.0: Finding the first line that goes wrong in a solution
y-m-72-03.thinking.1: Building a counterexample to a plausible conclusion
y-m-72-03.thinking.2: Explaining how the rule is applied
y-m-72-03.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Percentage calculation and the experience of reading an amount of money split into brackets (about Grade 7 to 8 level). This task is at an introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.prompt: This is Seoyun's solution. Reading it with the rule above, choose the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write what 'the amount that belongs to a bracket' means in the rule, by splitting 4,100만원 into two parts.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.hint.1: Find directly, by the rule, the after-tax income at 4,000만원 and at 4,100만원 and compare.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.line.0: Annual income 4,000만원: tax 4,000×10% = 400만원, so after-tax income is 3,600만원.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.line.1: Annual income 4,100만원: it went over 4,000만원, so 20% is applied to the whole income of 4,100만원.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.line.3: Income rose by 100만원 but after-tax income fell by 320만원, so the moment you cross a bracket you actually lose.
y-m-72-03.s.s1.explain: The first line follows the rule. The place where it goes wrong is line 2. The rule applies each rate only to 'the amount that belongs to that bracket', but this solution applied the new rate to the whole income. The calculation in line 3 just followed line 2, and the conclusion in line 4 was built on that wrong application, so it collapses with it. By the rule, the tax on 4,100만원 is 400만원 (for the part up to 4,000만원) plus 20만원 (20% of the 100만원 over), which is 420만원.
y-m-72-03.s.s2.hint.0: Take a to be 4,000만원 or less and b a little more than 4,000만원, and calculate the tax by splitting it into brackets.
y-m-72-03.s.s2.ok.c1: Both incomes are integers from 1,000 to 20,000만원, and b is greater than a.
y-m-72-03.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be an integer of at least 1,000, b an integer of at most 20,000, and b must be greater than a.
y-m-72-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The average tax rate at b is higher than at a.
y-m-72-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The average tax rate (tax ÷ income) at b is not higher than at a. Check whether the two incomes are both in the same bracket.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Seoyun. Put in numbers for the tax when income is 4,100만원, write where the new rate of 20% applies, and say in one or two sentences why Seoyun's statement 'if you cross a bracket you lose' is wrong.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.hint.0: First write which part of the income the amount multiplied by 20% in the solution above is.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write the after-tax incomes at 4,000만원 and at 4,100만원 side by side and make a sentence comparing them.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I make clear which part, not the whole income, the 20% applies to?
y-m-72-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I show with numbers that after-tax income did not decrease?
y-m-72-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I kindly point out where Seoyun misunderstood?
y-m-72-03.s.s3.model.0: With 4,100만원, the part up to 4,000만원 is at 10%, which is 400만원, and 20% applies only to the 100만원 over, which is 20만원. The tax is 420만원 and the after-tax income is 3,680만원, so it actually went up.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.model.1: The 20% applies only to the part over the bracket. For 4,100만원 it is 20% on only 100만원, so the tax is 420만원, and the after-tax 3,680만원 is more than the after-tax 3,600만원 at 4,000만원. So it is not a loss.
y-m-72-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: I showed the numbers and the comparison together.

y-m-72-05.title: Is a draw with big prizes really a good deal for players?
y-m-72-05.topic: Expected value and designing a fair game
y-m-72-05.goal: Evaluate a draw by the average prize value that takes both the prize values and the chance of being drawn into account, design boxes that fit the conditions yourself, and explain the difference between one result and the average.
y-m-72-05.material:
A draw box at the school festival has 20 balls. The fee for one draw is 1,000원, and you receive a prize by drawing one ball at random (the drawn ball is put back, so the conditions are the same each time). Prize values are counted by the amount the class paid.
1 gold ball: 5,000원 worth / 3 silver balls: 2,000원 worth / 4 bronze balls: 500원 worth / 12 blanks: 0원
(Read: 5,000원, 2,000원, 500원.) A player, Minjae, said, 'There is a gold ball, so this draw is a good deal for players.'
y-m-72-05.thinking.2: Telling apart luck and the average
y-m-72-05.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience of describing a chance as 'how many out of the total' (fractions and ratios, about Grade 7 to 8 level). The assumption is given that the drawn ball is put back so the chances are the same. This task is at an introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.prompt: Minjae says, 'There is a gold ball, so this draw is a good deal for players.' What is the most suitable thing to do to find out whether this is right?
y-m-72-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each kind of ball, find and write 'prize value × chance of being drawn (how many out of 20)'.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the total of those values is greater or less than the fee of 1,000원.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.o.a: Work out the average amount received by considering prize values and chances and compare it with the fee
y-m-72-05.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that tries to compare the average amount received per draw over many draws with the fee.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.o.b: The chance of the gold ball looks small, so it is a loss for players
y-m-72-05.s.s1.r.b: A small chance alone is not enough. You must also consider how large the value is when the gold ball comes out.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.o.c: Decide whether it is a good deal by looking at the results of two or three friends who drew first
y-m-72-05.s.s1.r.c: The results of a few people depend greatly on luck. You need a way to work out what happens when many people draw.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.o.d: There are 12 blanks, so it is surely a loss for players
y-m-72-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if there are many blanks, the average can be large if there is a big prize. You cannot reach a conclusion from the number of balls alone.
y-m-72-05.s.s1.explain: The average prize value received per draw is (5,000×1 + 2,000×3 + 500×4 + 0×12) ÷ 20 = 650원. It is less than the fee of 1,000원, so if many people draw, a player loses 350원 per draw on average and the operator keeps that much. If you play only once, you might draw the gold ball and come out ahead.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.prompt: This time, become the operator and set up the box yourself. There are 20 balls in all and at least 1 must be a blank. With at most 2 gold balls, choose the numbers of gold balls g, silver balls s and bronze balls b so that the average prize value per draw is at least 700원 and at most 900원, and make three different boxes. (Prize values: gold 5,000원, silver 2,000원, bronze 500원)
y-m-72-05.s.s2.hint.0: First find what the total of the prize values of all 20 balls must be for the average to be 700원 and 900원.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the number of gold balls, then change the numbers of silver and bronze balls and check whether the total falls in that range.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of balls are integers of at least 0.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the numbers of balls integers of at least 0.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Gold, silver and bronze balls number more than 19, so there are no blanks.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.ok.c3: There are at most 2 gold balls.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Please make the gold balls at most 2.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The average prize value is at least 700원.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.fail.c4: The average prize value falls short of 700원. This is a box where the operator keeps too much.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.ok.c5: The average prize value is at most 900원.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.fail.c5: The average prize value exceeds 900원. This is a box where the operator hardly keeps anything.
y-m-72-05.s.s2.explain: If the total of the prize values of the 20 balls is at least 14,000원 and at most 18,000원, the average is 700 to 900원. For example, 2 gold and 2 silver (16 blanks) is 10,000+4,000=14,000원, an average of 700원, and 2 gold, 3 silver and 4 bronze is 18,000원, an average of 900원. Even with the same average, a box with big prizes and a box with many small prizes feel different.
y-m-72-05.s.s3.prompt: Even if a player draws the 5,000원 gold ball in a single draw, the operator can say 'on average we come out ahead.' Explain the reason using numbers.
y-m-72-05.s.s3.hint.0: Separate the one person who drew the gold ball from the whole group of 1,000 who drew, and write what is how much for each.
y-m-72-05.s.s3.hint.1: Find and compare the money the operator received and the prize value given out when 1,000 people drew.
y-m-72-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: One person ... but if many draw ...
y-m-72-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I write the difference between luck on a single draw and the average over many draws?

y-m-72-06.title: Does the loan with the smaller monthly burden also have less total interest?
y-m-72-06.topic: Comparing loan repayment methods (monthly burden and total interest)
y-m-72-06.goal: Confirm by calculation that a smaller monthly payment and less total interest are different things, and explain with numbers that the choice can split because the important condition differs from person to person.
y-m-72-06.material:
We compare three ways of repaying 1,200만원 over 12 months. Assume the monthly interest rate is 0.5% (an approximation of 6% a year divided by 12), interest is charged each month on the principal remaining just before repayment, and there are no fees.
A (bullet repayment): pay only the interest each month, and pay back the principal of 1,200만원 all at once in month 12.
B (equal principal): each month pay 100만원 of principal together with the interest on that month's remaining principal.
C (equal principal and interest): pay the same amount each month (about 1,032,797원).
The first month's payments are A 60,000원, B 1,060,000원, C about 1,032,797원. Seoyun said, 'The method with the smaller monthly payment should also have less total interest.' (Read: zero point five percent, 1,200만원.)

(Read: C of q equals q squared plus 4 q plus 100.) Below are a few values.
q=2: 56 / q=4: 33 / q=6: about 26.7 / q=8: 24.5
The factory manager says, 'The more we make, the lower the cost per box, so let's make as many as possible.'

y-m-72-10.material: This is a model that simplifies the daily trade of one kind of fruit in a neighborhood market into linear expressions. The price P is in 천원 per item, the quantity demanded is Qd = 100 − 2P, and the quantity supplied is Qs = −20 + 4P (items). Trade takes place at the price where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied (equilibrium). The government put a tax of 6천원 per item on the seller. The consumer pays the price P, and the seller receives P−6, which is what remains after paying the tax of 6. Seoyun solved it as below, with the idea that 'even if the seller is taxed, the price the consumer pays goes up by the amount of the tax'.
y-m-72-10.thinking.0: Finding where the solution goes wrong because of an assumption
y-m-72-10.thinking.1: Checking the solution for consistency (quantity demanded = quantity supplied)
y-m-72-10.thinking.2: Making results that change with conditions
y-m-72-10.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience of solving two linear expressions together (about high-school mathematics). The convention that trade takes place at the price where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied is given in the material. This task is one step higher than introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.prompt: This is Seoyun's solution. Choose the one line that goes against the rule and throws off the conclusion. (Read: 100 minus 2P.)
y-m-72-10.s.s1.hint.0: Find the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied at 26천원 and check whether they are the same.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write the money the seller receives after the tax in terms of P and set up the supply expression again.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.line.0: Before tax: from 100−2P = −20+4P, P = 20 and the quantity traded is 60.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.line.1: The tax of 6천원 is all paid by the consumer, so the new price is P = 20+6 = 26.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.line.2: If P = 26, the quantity demanded is 100−2×26 = 48.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.line.3: At this point the money the seller receives is 26−6 = 20천원, and the quantity supplied is −20+4×20 = 60.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the quantity traded after tax is 48, and the consumer bears the whole tax of 6천원.
y-m-72-10.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the problem. It decided in advance that 'the consumer pays the whole tax'. As a result, at 26천원 the quantity demanded (48) and the quantity supplied (60) differ, and yet it said the trade goes ahead anyway (you can see this by comparing lines 3 and 4). At a price where trade takes place, the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied must be equal. The conclusion in line 5 is also wrong because of this. After the tax, the seller receives P−6, so the quantity supplied is −20+4(P−6), and solving 100−2P = −20+4(P−6) gives P = 24 and a quantity traded of 52. The consumer bears 4천원 (20→24) and the seller bears 2천원 (20→18).
y-m-72-10.s.s2.prompt: In a market with quantity demanded Qd = 100 − aP and quantity supplied Qs = −20 + bP, the seller is taxed 6천원 per item. Make three different pairs (a, b) for which the price the consumer pays goes up by at least 5천원 of the 6천원 tax. (a is an integer from 1 to 5, b is an integer from 1 to 30, and the quantity traded must still be greater than 0 after the tax.)
y-m-72-10.s.s2.hint.0: For the market with a=2, b=4 (Seoyun's solution market), first find how much the consumer price went up and use it as a reference.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.hint.1: Make a small and b large, do the same calculation, and look at how the amount the price goes up changes.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.var.a: How much the quantity demanded responds to price (a)
y-m-72-10.s.s2.var.b: How much the quantity supplied responds to price (b)
y-m-72-10.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a an integer from 1 to 5 and b an integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The price the consumer pays goes up by at least 5천원.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The consumer price does not go up by at least 5천원. Write the equilibrium price after tax in terms of a and b and compare it with the original price.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.ok.c3: The quantity traded is still greater than 0 after the tax.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.fail.c3: The quantity traded after the tax is 0 or less. Find the equilibrium after the tax and check whether the quantity traded is positive.
y-m-72-10.s.s2.explain: The equilibrium price before tax is 120÷(a+b), and after tax it is (120+6b)÷(a+b), so the consumer price goes up by 6b÷(a+b). 6b÷(a+b)≥5 is the same as b≥5a. Example: if a=1, b=5, the consumer price goes up by 5천원. The more the quantity supplied responds to price and the less sensitive the quantity demanded is to price, the more of the tax the consumer bears.
y-m-72-10.s.s3.prompt: In Seoyun's market (a=2, b=4), the consumer bore only 4천원 of the 6천원 tax. Using numbers, explain what was different in the examples in s2 where the consumer bore almost all of it (5천원 or more).
y-m-72-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write down and place side by side the equilibrium prices before and after tax for the two markets a=2, b=4 and a=1, b=5.
y-m-72-10.s.s3.hint.1: Put into words which of a and b became larger and whether that increases the response of the quantity demanded or of the quantity supplied.
y-m-72-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When a=2, b=4, ..., and when a=1, b=5, ...
y-m-72-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I include the numbers both for when the consumer's burden is 4천원 and when it is 5천원 or more?
y-m-72-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain that the burden is split depending on whether the demand side or the supply side is more sensitive to price?
y-m-72-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I think that who legally pays the tax and who actually bears it can differ?
y-m-72-10.s.s3.model.0: When a=2, b=4, the consumer price went up by 4천원, but with a=1, b=5 it goes up by 5천원. The less the quantity demanded responds to price and the more the quantity supplied responds to price, the more of the tax the consumer bears.
y-m-72-10.s.s3.model.1: If the quantity supplied is very sensitive to price, sellers easily cut back on selling because of the tax, so in a market where buyers have to buy even if the price goes up, the consumer bears most of it. If a=1, b=8, the consumer price goes up by about 5.3천원.
y-m-72-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: I explained the reason through the seller's response.

y-m-72-11.title: If sales rose after advertising, was it thanks to the advertising?
y-m-72-11.topic: Estimating a cause from comparison data (sales before and after advertising)
y-m-72-11.goal: Confirm that the fact that sales rose after advertising alone cannot tell you the effect of advertising, and that looking together at the shop that did not advertise and the trend before advertising changes the estimate of the effect, and revise your judgment and confidence.
y-m-72-11.material: Shop A and shop B of a snack-shop chain are in different neighborhoods of the same city. In the third quarter of this year, only shop A advertised online and shop B did not. Quarterly sales are revealed step by step in units of 백만원. The effect of advertising is taken to be 'the size of the increase in the sales growth rate that came from the advertising', and the unit is the percentage point (%p, the difference between two rates). (Read: 280백만원, percentage point.)
y-m-72-11.thinking.0: Revising your judgment and confidence each time data increases
y-m-72-11.thinking.1: Examining whether the comparison object is suitable
y-m-72-11.thinking.2: Pointing out what is not yet known
y-m-72-11.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience of finding a rate of increase (%) and telling a percentage difference (%p) apart (about high-school mathematics). This task is one step higher than introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your judgment about 'the effect of the advertising'. The effect of advertising is taken as 'the size of the increase in the sales growth rate that came from the advertising (percentage points, %p)'.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.hint.0: In a table, write each shop's earlier sales and later sales, and write the rate of increase as a percent.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.hint.1: Find the difference in the rate of increase between the shop that advertised and the one that did not, then compare whether there was such a difference before the advertising too.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.info: Shop A, which advertised, had quarterly sales that rose from 280백만원 in the second quarter to 322백만원 in the third quarter (+15%). There is no other data yet.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only what is known now, how would you describe the effect of the advertising?
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.after: The fact that sales rose after advertising alone does not tell you whether it was thanks to the advertising. You need to know how much of the rise would have happened without advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I think it increased by 15%p because of the advertising
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 15% is the whole size of the rise in sales. There is not yet any data that tells how much would have risen even without advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There seems to be an effect, but I do not yet know its size
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that guesses the direction from the clue that sales rose after advertising, but says the size can be decided only when there is data to compare with.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There is no data to compare with, so I cannot yet decide whether there was an effect
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that points out that the amount of the rise without advertising cannot be known.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I think the rise was because of the season
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It may be because of the season. But with the current data alone there is no basis to assert that it was because of the season either.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.info: Shop B, which did not advertise in the same period, had quarterly sales that rose from 275 to 302.5백만원 (+10%).
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: How would you estimate the size of the advertising effect?
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.after: Subtracting shop B's 10%, which rose without advertising, from shop A's 15% gives about 5%p. This estimate treats shop B as the comparison group for 'the part that rises without advertising'.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a value that used shop A's rate of increase as it was. It did not take into account that shop B also rose without advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Adding the rates of increase of shop A and shop B is not the size of the advertising effect.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is shop A's 15% minus shop B's 10%, which rose even without advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 0%p. Shop B rose too, so the advertising is useless
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Shop B having risen means there is a part that rises without advertising; it does not mean that shop A's larger increase has nothing to do with the advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.info: In the earlier period, before either advertised (quarter 1 to 2), shop A went from 250 to 280, +12%, and shop B went from 250 to 275, +10%.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: Seeing this data, how would you estimate the size of the advertising effect?
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.after: Subtracting the original gap (2%p) from the post-advertising gap (5%p) gives about 3%p. However, if you think the original gap is the value of just one quarter and may be chance, you can also keep it near 5%p. The more data, the finer the estimate, but if other factors (such as neighborhood events) remain, confidence has limits.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Keep it at about 5%p. The 2%p gap in one quarter may be chance
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a judgment that kept the estimate, taking into account that the gap in the one preceding quarter may be chance. Your confidence may have gone down.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Reduce it to about 3%p. Shop A was already growing 2%p faster
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is an estimate that subtracts the 2%p gap from when there was no advertising from 5%p.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Increase it to about 7%p. Count shop A's original gap as advertising effect too
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: If you add the gap that was already there to the effect, the effect is inflated.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.o.d: There is no effect. Because shop A was growing faster all along
y-m-72-11.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The original gap is 2%p and the gap after advertising is 5%p. Since the gap grew, it is hard to say the advertising had no effect at all.
y-m-72-11.s.s1.reflect: Your estimate of the advertising effect changed from '15%p or unknown' to 'about 5%p' to 'about 3 to 5%p'. Say what data changed the estimate at each step, and what still makes this estimate hard to trust.
y-m-72-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write one thing you would like to know more about in order to say shop B is similar to shop A.
y-m-72-11.s.s2.hint.1: Think of one thing that may have happened only at shop A at the same time as the advertising.
y-m-72-11.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If there was ... in shop A's neighborhood, then ...
y-m-72-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the two things not yet known of different kinds (for example, the neighborhood's circumstances and a chance gap)?
y-m-72-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I write in which direction each could change the conclusion?
y-m-72-11.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I think about how far I can say shop B is a shop similar to shop A?
y-m-72-11.s.s2.model.0: If there was a big event in shop A's neighborhood in the same period, the rise in sales may not be because of the advertising, so the effect could be smaller than 3%p. Also, the difference in the shops' usual growth was seen for only one quarter, so if it was chance, the estimate could move toward 5%p.
y-m-72-11.s.s2.model.1: If shop B differs from shop A in menu or customers, shop B cannot stand in for the part that rises without advertising, so the estimate could be wrong. If there was something other than the advertising, like a price change, that could also have an influence and change the effect.
y-m-72-11.s.s2.modelNote.1: I pointed out whether the comparison object is suitable.

y-m-72-12.topic: Price competition between two shops (reading and designing a payoff table)
y-m-72-12.goal: Confirm with a payoff table that even when one choice is better whatever the other does, if both do it together it can be worse for everyone, design a payoff table of the same structure yourself, and say how things change when it is repeated, with conditions.
y-m-72-12.material:
Snack shop X and snack shop Y are on the same street, and for one week each can either 'keep' or 'cut' its price. The two shops decide at the same time and do not know each other's choice. (Agreeing on prices beforehand (collusion) is often prohibited by law, so it is not covered in this task.) The profits for one week (만원; the order is X's profit, Y's profit) are as follows.
X keeps · Y keeps: (60, 60)
X cuts · Y keeps: (80, 30)
X keeps · Y cuts: (30, 80)
X cuts · Y cuts: (40, 40)
(Read: if X cuts and Y keeps, X gets 80만원 and Y gets 30만원.)
y-m-72-12.thinking.0: Reading the table and comparing by each choice of the other
y-m-72-12.thinking.1: Making an example of the same structure under constraints
y-m-72-12.thinking.2: Explaining the difference between a one-time and a repeated situation with conditions
y-m-72-12.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience of reading a table, comparing sizes and checking inequality conditions (about high-school mathematics). This task is one step higher than introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-12.s.s1.prompt: Think from shop X's point of view. Whatever shop Y chooses (keep or cut), which choice is better for X?
y-m-72-12.s.s1.hint.0: When Y keeps, find the two values of X's profit in the table and compare them.
y-m-72-12.s.s1.hint.1: Also find the two values of X's profit when Y cuts and compare them, and check whether the results of the two comparisons are the same.
y-m-72-12.s.s1.explain: If Y keeps, X's cut (80) is greater than keeping (60), and if Y cuts, X's cut (40) is greater than keeping (30). Whatever Y does, cutting is better, so X wants to choose cutting. Y has the same structure, so if both cut it is (40, 40), even though both keeping gave the larger (60, 60).
y-m-72-12.s.s2.prompt: Make another payoff table with the same structure as above yourself. T is X's profit when only X cuts, R when both keep, P when both cut, and S when only X keeps (only Y cuts). To keep the structure of the story, T > R > P > S must hold, and the sum of the profit and loss from only one side cutting (T+S) must be less than twice the profit from both keeping (2R). Make two different sets of four values that differ from the table above. (Integers from 0 to 100)
y-m-72-12.s.s2.hint.0: First write the order of size of the four numbers in the table above.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.hint.1: Change the numbers while keeping the order, and check the last condition (2R versus T+S) by calculating it yourself.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.var.T: X's profit when only X cuts (T)
y-m-72-12.s.s2.var.S: X's profit when only X keeps (S)
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c1: The four values are integers from 0 to 100.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the four values integers from 0 to 100.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c2: The profit T from cutting alone is greater than R for both keeping.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c2: T is not greater than R. When the other keeps, cutting must be more profitable.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c3: Both keeping (R) is greater than both cutting (P).
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c3: R is not greater than P. If both cut, both must be worse off.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c4: Both cutting (P) is greater than keeping alone (S).
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c4: P is not greater than S. When the other cuts, cutting must also be more profitable.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c5: The sum when both keep (2R) is greater than the sum when only one cuts (T+S).
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c5: 2R is not greater than T+S. The sum when both keep must be larger.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.ok.c6: They are numbers different from the table above.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.fail.c6: They are the same numbers as the table above. Make them with different numbers.
y-m-72-12.s.s2.explain: If T>R>P>S as in (70, 50, 20, 10) and 2R=100 is greater than T+S=80, the structure of the story is the same. In this structure each shop profits by choosing to cut, yet if both cut, the profit is smaller than if both had kept.
y-m-72-12.s.s3.prompt: If these two shops compete not just once but continue to compete every week, could the conclusion change? Write, with reasons, under what conditions it could change and how (or that it would not change).
y-m-72-12.s.s3.hint.0: Write whether your choice this week would change when you learn that the other shop cut last week.
y-m-72-12.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how 'how will the other react if I cut?' differs between competing only once and continuing to compete.
y-m-72-12.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If they compete every week ...
y-m-72-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I think that when it is repeated you can decide by looking at the other's past choices?
y-m-72-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I write concretely the conditions under which the conclusion could change (the other's reaction, trust and so on)?
y-m-72-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I think that there may be cases where it does not change (such as when the last week is fixed)?
y-m-72-12.s.s3.model.0: If they keep competing every week, they can look at whether the other cut last week and cut together next week, so both keeping can continue, or mutual cutting can become fixed. So the conclusion can change depending on the other's reaction.
y-m-72-12.s.s3.model.1: If it is only once, cutting is better, but if it is repeated over many weeks the other may retaliate and profits may fall, so you might choose to keep. However, if both know the last week is fixed, they will cut in the last week, so the conclusion could change again.

y-m-72-13.title: Can we talk about five years ahead from three years of records?
y-m-72-13.topic: Comparing trend models and limits of prediction (linear and exponential)
y-m-72-13.goal: Learn that when the records fit both models you cannot choose between them, find for yourself the time at which the two models split, and say what information would let you tell the models apart.
y-m-72-13.material:
A shop's annual sales (억원) were 100 in year 1, 122 in year 2 and 144 in year 3. Because of the way they are counted, each value may have an error of about ±2억원. Taking year 1 as t=0, t=0, 1, 2 are the three years above. Two people set up models.
Model L: it increases by 22억원 every year. L(t) = 100 + 22t
Model E: it increases by 20% every year. E(t) = 100 × 1.2^t
(Read: L of t equals 100 plus 22 t; E of t equals 100 times 1.2 to the power t.) At t=0, 1, 2, L is 100, 122, 144 and E is 100, 120, 144.
y-m-72-13.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-72-13.thinking.1: Comparing models and checking predictions beyond the records
y-m-72-13.thinking.2: Saying what additional information is needed
y-m-72-13.prereq.0: (Assignment assumption) 'Economic Mathematics' is assumed to be a high-school elective chosen after learning the basics of numbers, expressions and functions. H1/H2 are only difficulty and support level labels for this production assignment; they do not mean the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Experience of substituting values into a linear expression a+bt and an exponential expression a·r^t (about high-school mathematics). This task is one step higher than introductory difficulty.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.prompt: The two models L and E fit the three years of records like this. L fits exactly with 100, 122, 144, and E fits within 2억원 with 100, 120, 144. The records may have an error of ±2억원. What is the suitable thing to say?
y-m-72-13.s.s1.hint.0: Write the values of L and E at t=1, 2 next to the records and find the differences.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether those differences fall within the error of ±2억원.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.o.a: L fits the three values exactly, so L is the right model
y-m-72-13.s.s1.r.a: Fitting exactly does not mean it is the right model. If the records have error, fitting exactly could even be strange.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.r.b: It was said that the records may have an error of ±2억원. It is hard to say a model is wrong because of a difference within that.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.o.c: Considering the error too, we cannot choose between the two models from these records alone
y-m-72-13.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that points out that both models fit within the error range of the records.
y-m-72-13.s.s1.explain: The records of the three years fit both L and E within the error range. So these records alone cannot tell which model is right. But the predictions of the two models can differ greatly in the far future.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.prompt: We want to see how much the predictions of L and E differ. Find three different values of t (years elapsed) at which E's prediction is at least 10% greater than L's prediction. (t is an integer from 3 to 10)
y-m-72-13.s.s2.hint.0: Find the values of L and E at t=3, 4, 5 and compare E÷L as decimals.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.hint.1: After finding the first t where E÷L exceeds 1.1, check a few more larger t to see whether it keeps exceeding.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.var.t: Number of years t elapsed since year 1
y-m-72-13.s.s2.ok.c1: t is an integer from 3 to 10.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make t an integer from 3 to 10.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.ok.c2: E's prediction is at least 10% greater than L's prediction.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.fail.c2: E's prediction falls short of 1.1 times L's. Find the values of the two models at that t and compare them.
y-m-72-13.s.s2.explain: At t=3, L is 166 and E is about 172.8, a difference of only about 4%. At t=4, L is 188 and E is about 207.4, a difference of more than 10% (about 10.3%). In the range with records the two models are almost the same, and the farther you go beyond the records, the more the predictions split.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information that would help in choosing one of the two models.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.hint.0: From the results of s2, find when the two models split the most.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.hint.1: Write how you could tell which model the actual value at that time is closer to, if it existed.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.o.a: The actual sales in year 4 and year 5
y-m-72-13.s.s3.r.a: At values beyond the records the two models split greatly, so once actual values come out you can tell which one they are closer to.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.o.b: Which of the expressions of the two models is simpler
y-m-72-13.s.s3.r.b: A simple expression does not mean it describes reality better. It is a separate matter from which one is right.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.o.c: How much larger the market of the neighborhood where this shop does business can become
y-m-72-13.s.s3.r.c: It tells whether it is an environment in which sales can keep growing at the same rate. If the market has a limit, it is hard to keep growing like E.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.o.d: Values of the three years measured again more accurately (with smaller error)
y-m-72-13.s.s3.r.d: If the error shrinks, the difference between 122 and 120 at t=1 can become meaningful. You can tell which one it is closer to.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.explain: Actual values at times beyond the records (years 4 and 5) and values of the same period measured more accurately are direct evidence that separates the two models. How much larger the market can become does not tell which model is 'right', but it tells the range in which a prediction is valid, so it is worth considering together. Whether the expression is simple has nothing to do with which model is right.
y-m-72-13.s.s3.acc.0: How much larger the market can become does not separate which model is right, but it tells how far a prediction can be trusted. It is reasonable to consider it together.
